title: From Chairside Assistant to Digital Fabrication Specialist: The Evolution of the Dental Team
html:
By Chelsea Homire, DA

November 23, 2026

Share

The integration of intraoral scanning, CAD/CAM, and additive manufacturing has changed how dental restorations and appliances are produced. Digital workflows allow practices to capture patient data, design restorations, and fabricate appliances with greater control over the production process. Research has demonstrated advantages in clinical efficiency and patient experience for selected applications.¹,²

However, implementing digital technology involves more than purchasing equipment. Every workflow requires someone to manage digital files, evaluate designs, operate fabrication equipment, and oversee post-processing and quality control. As more of these responsibilities move into dental practices, the roles of the dental team are beginning to change.

The Emergence of the Digital Fabrication Specialist

Dental assistants have always worn multiple hats. From assisting with procedures to managing patients, materials, and equipment, adaptability is part of the profession. Digital dentistry is creating another opportunity to expand their responsibilities.

An emerging role, often described as the Digital Fabrication Specialist (DFS), combines clinical knowledge with digital design and laboratory fabrication skills. Although the title is not yet a standardized professional designation, it reflects a growing need within practices bringing production in-house.

A trained DFS may manage digital scans, prepare designs, operate 3D printers and milling equipment, and complete appropriate finishing and quality-control procedures. More importantly, they understand how these steps connect, from the initial scan to final delivery. Rather than simply operating equipment, they help manage the entire production workflow.

The Advantage of Understanding Both Sides

One of the greatest advantages dental assistants bring to digital fabrication is their clinical experience.

Consider an occlusal guard. The assistant may have been present during the patient's initial appointment, captured the scans, recorded the bite, and observed the patient's occlusion. They may also understand the dentist's preferences and the patient's concerns.

When that same assistant is trained to design and fabricate the guard, they bring that clinical knowledge into production.

If the appliance doesn't fit, they can begin troubleshooting. Was the scan accurate? Was the bite registration correct? Did the design provide adequate clearance? Could printing or post-processing have affected the fit? These aren't simply laboratory questions. They connect directly to what happened clinically.

The same principle applies to dentures, provisional restorations, and other appliances. An assistant who understands both sides of the process may recognize missing information or potential problems before the patient returns.

This doesn't replace the expertise of dental laboratory technicians. Instead, it creates another knowledgeable team member who can communicate with the dentist and laboratory while helping maintain continuity throughout treatment.

Taking Work Off the Dentist's Plate

One challenge with bringing digital fabrication in-house is deciding who will actually do the work.

A dentist may invest in a scanner, printer, and design software expecting greater efficiency, only to find themselves designing guards after the last patient leaves, coming in early to remove prints, or staying late to finish a denture.

The technology may save time in one area while creating additional work in another. A properly trained DFS can take responsibility for appropriate portions of production. The dentist remains responsible for diagnosis, treatment planning, clinical decisions, and required approvals, but doesn't necessarily need to complete every technical step.

Design preparation, print scheduling, post-processing, equipment maintenance, and routine quality-control checks can become organized responsibilities rather than tasks squeezed between patients.

A DFS can also establish repeatable workflows, help train other team members, and troubleshoot production problems, allowing the dentist to focus more time on patient care.

Practice Efficiency and Patient Experience

In-house fabrication can offer shorter turnaround times, greater production control, and fewer shipping delays. Depending on case volume and operating costs, it may also reduce laboratory expenses.

However, purchasing equipment doesn't automatically make a practice more efficient or profitable. Materials, maintenance, labor, training, and remakes must all be considered.

A trained DFS can help reduce preventable errors, keep production organized, and identify problems before delivery. In selected workflows, this may mean fewer adjustments, less chair time, and fewer appointments.

Patients also appreciate convenience. Research comparing digital and conventional impressions has found that patients generally prefer intraoral scanning, with advantages in comfort and, in many applications, procedure time.²

The goal isn't necessarily to fabricate everything in-house. It's to identify which procedures make clinical and financial sense and develop a team capable of completing them consistently.

A New Career Path for Dental Assistants

For dental assistants, this evolving role offers more than additional daily responsibilities.

Many assistants enjoy dentistry but eventually want to learn something new, take on greater responsibility, or increase their earning potential. Others may feel they've reached a ceiling in their careers.

Digital fabrication offers opportunities to develop specialized skills in design, technology, and problem-solving without leaving the clinical environment. These skills may support professional advancement and compensation discussions. Just as importantly, learning a different side of dentistry can renew an assistant's interest in a career they've spent years building.

Looking Ahead

As digital dentistry becomes more integrated into everyday practice, the responsibilities of the dental team will continue to evolve. Developing a DFS requires education, hands-on experience, clear protocols, and an understanding of state-specific scope-of-practice requirements.

The next big advancement in digital dentistry may not be another printer, scanner, or design software. It may be recognizing what the people already working in our practices are capable of learning.

Author Bio:

Chelsea Homire is a dental fabrication specialist and clinical educator focused on advancing digital workflows, CAD design, and 3D printing in modern dental practice. As a passionate advocate for dental team development, she collaborates with clinicians, laboratories, and industry partners to bridge the gap between technology and practical application.
